title: The People Who Build Their Own Islands. Every Few Months.
question: Why do people live on the Uros floating islands?
message: This video tells curious adults that the Uros people live on islands they build themselves from reeds on Lake Titicaca, because the lake gave them food, safety and a home that could move, and today it also gives them a living.
angle: People live on the Uros islands because, as their history is usually told, moving onto the lake kept them safe, and totora reeds give them islands, houses and boats while the lake gives fish and birds, and now tourism keeps the islands going, despite floors that rot from below, an island that has to be rebuilt every few decades, thin air at almost four thousand metres and limited clean water.

scenes.narration: The lake is Titicaca, on the border of Peru and Bolivia. The people are the Uros. Their islands are not rock, not sand, not land at all. They are made of totora, a thick reed that grows in the lake, piled layer on layer until you can build a house on it. And the floor never stays finished. Once you know that, the obvious question is why anyone would choose a home that needs rebuilding from the top down. By the end of this trip I had my answer. I also had one very wet leg, which I will explain later, with as much dignity as I can find.

scenes.narration: The boat from Puno takes about half an hour, and the islands are only about five kilometres from the port. Up close, they look like giant golden mattresses floating on dark blue water, with little reed houses sitting on top. I stepped off the boat with great confidence. The ground went down. Then it came back up. It felt like walking on a sponge that had opinions. I bounced to the middle of the island, proud of myself. Then I took a step toward the edge, where the reeds were older, and my leg went straight through into the lake. Up to the knee. Cold. Very cold. Lonely Planet actually warns visitors about this. I had not read that part. I read it now, sitting on the reeds, with one dry leg and one educated leg.

scenes.narration: Here is what my leg had discovered. These islands rot from the bottom. Water slowly breaks down the lowest layers of reed, so islanders keep adding fresh reeds on top. On the busier islands, that means a new layer about every three months, and more often in the rainy season. Even with all that care, an island lasts around thirty years before people have to build a new one from scratch. There is even a strange bonus. According to a Stanford researcher quoted by Smithsonian, rotting reeds produce gases, including carbon dioxide and methane, and those gases may help keep the islands floating. Picture a bed where the bottom mattress slowly melts away, so every few months you lay a fresh one on top. You never stop making the bed. The bed is the house.

scenes.narration: So why live on water at all, with solid ground right there on the shore? My guess was fishing. Live on the lake, sleep next to your dinner. That is part of it, but it is not the story people usually tell. The Uros have lived on this lake for hundreds of years. According to the most common account, they moved out onto floating islands when the Inca Empire expanded onto their land. An island made of reeds has a huge advantage over an island made of rock. If trouble comes, you can untie it and move. Smithsonian puts it simply: they made islands they could move if things got tense. Imagine a house where, if the neighbours get difficult, you pull up the anchor and float somewhere quieter.

scenes.role: chương 3: từ một cọng lau → bó → thuyền → nhà → đảo; khối rễ khili buộc, neo
scenes.narration: Then I watched someone show visitors how an island is made, and I zoomed out in my head. Start with one reed. Hollow, light, a little spongy. Tie a big armful together and you get a bundle that floats. Tie bundles together and you get a boat, with curved ends, sometimes with a carved animal head at the front. Weave the reeds flat and you get walls, and then a little house with a pointed roof. Zoom out again. Under it all, the island itself sits on big floating blocks of totora roots. They are tied together with rope and anchored, so the island does not drift off in the night. Then come the layers of cut reeds, again and again. So the reed is the floor, the walls, the roof and the transport. Almost nothing here is not reed, except the lake, and the lake is where the reeds grow.

scenes.narration: Next I discovered the other thing about this place. It is high. Very high. Lake Titicaca sits at about three thousand eight hundred and ten metres. That's around twelve thousand five hundred feet. Britannica calls it the world's highest lake navigable by large vessels. Picture climbing a staircase while someone quietly takes away part of the air. I walked to the edge of the island to look at the view and had to sit down halfway. The lake, though, is generous. The reed beds around these islands are part of the Titicaca National Reserve. It protects about thirty-seven thousand hectares of reeds, with around sixty kinds of birds and fourteen kinds of fish. The Uros have long used many of them for meat and eggs. And for the rest, there is trade. Islanders barter with merchants from Puno for meat and vegetables.

scenes.narration: Life here has real costs. Discover magazine notes that clean water is limited on the islands. Everything you build needs constant care. And at this height the sun is fierce in the day and the nights get cold. I stayed until sunset anyway. The water went from blue to silver to black, and then the stars came out, more of them than I have ever seen from anywhere with a roof. Reed houses creaked softly as the island moved with the water, like a ship asleep at anchor. I lay on my back on the reeds, which were warm from the sun, and thought, I understand this. A home you build yourself, on water that feeds you, under a sky like that. I changed my mind. Maybe I could learn to bounce.

scenes.chapter: A Day of Making the Floor
scenes.role: chương 5: một ngày theo giờ: cắt lau, phơi, rải lớp mới; Wob giúp, hỏng; (mồi lại, nhạc hài)
scenes.narration: The next day I asked to help with the floor. Early morning: reeds are cut from the beds around the island, from boats, with long knives. I was given a knife and a boat. I was then politely given back to the island, without the knife or the boat. Mid-morning: the cut reeds are spread out to dry in the sun. Drying reeds is something I am excellent at. I sat next to them and watched. Noon: the dry reeds are laid in fresh layers across the island, crossing each other so the floor stays even. I laid my bundle very carefully. It was beautiful. It was also on top of my own shoe. Afternoon: I walked across the new layer. It was springy and dry and smelled like hay and lake. Right after a new layer goes down, the whole island feels brand new. Then the water starts working again.

scenes.chapter: The Storm, the City and the Visitors
scenes.role: chương 6: bão 1986, đảo dựng lại gần Puno; du lịch 80%; nhiều người sống ở Puno; điều tra 2011
scenes.narration: On my last day I drew a map in my notebook of where the islands have been. For a long time, many of them floated farther out on the lake. Then, after a devastating storm in nineteen eighty-six, Smithsonian reports, many Uros rebuilt their islands near Puno. That short boat ride changed everything. Visitors now come by the hundreds of thousands. Families take turns opening their homes to show how reed life works, and around eighty percent of the local population works in tourism. At the twenty eleven census, according to Culture Trip, about twelve hundred Uros were living on sixty-two islands near Puno. Many Uros also live in the city itself, and plenty of families move between the island and the shore for school, work and supplies. When tourism stopped during the pandemic, Discover magazine reported, the islands felt it hard. So the route on my map is not a line from the past to the present. It is a loop, from reeds to city and back again, every single day.

scenes.narration: So why stay on the islands at all, when Puno has solid streets? From everything I saw and read, the islands are the Uros' own. They built them, they maintain them, and they decide who steps on them. Most Uros today speak Aymara and Spanish, and their old Uru language has almost disappeared. But the reed islands carry the history in a way a language book cannot. Tourism pays for school, boats and supplies, and it also means the knowledge of how to build an island keeps getting used. On my way to the boat, feeling very wise, I stepped on an old patch near the edge. My leg went through again. Same leg. Same lake. Same cold. I changed my mind back. The islands make sense. I do not make sense on the islands.

scenes.chapter: Would I Live on a Reed?
scenes.role: về bàn: ghép các mảnh 'vì sao', phán quyết NOPE (lỗi ở Wob), callback bó lau, câu hỏi kéo bình luận
scenes.narration: So here is how the floor adds up. The lake offered safety, as the Uros' history is usually told, because an island of reeds can move. The reeds give them islands, houses and boats. The lake gives fish and birds, and the city across the water gives trade, school and visitors. In return, the floor never stops needing work, and an island has to be rebuilt every few decades. Would I move there? I would love to visit again, with sturdier shoes. But my verdict is NOPE, and the fault is my leg, not the island. It suits people who love the water, the sky and building things with their hands. It does not suit anyone who walks without looking down. I put the piece of floor on my desk. Every few months I add a new reed on top, just to be safe. Would you rebuild your own floor every season to live on a lake?

verdict.label: NOPE
verdict.reason: Thin air at about 3,810 metres and a floor that rots from below are too much for Wob's lungs and feet, though the Uros have every reason to keep building.

claims.quote: Somebody built that island by hand, out of this. On a lake high in the Andes, people still do.
claims.statement: The Uros people of Lake Titicaca, high in the Andes, build and maintain floating islands by hand from totora reeds.

claims.quote: The lake is Titicaca, on the border of Peru and Bolivia. The people are the Uros.
claims.statement: Lake Titicaca lies on the border of Peru and Bolivia and is home to the Uros people's floating islands.

claims.quote: They are made of totora, a thick reed that grows in the lake, piled layer on layer until you can build a house on it.
claims.statement: The Uros islands are made of layers of totora reeds, which grow in Lake Titicaca, and support reed houses.

claims.quote: The boat from Puno takes about half an hour, and the islands are only about five kilometres from the port.
claims.statement: The Uros islands lie about 5 km from the port of Puno, roughly a 30-minute boat ride.

claims.quote: Lonely Planet actually warns visitors about this.
claims.statement: Lonely Planet warns visitors to the Uros islands to be careful not to put a foot through rotten sections of reed.

claims.quote: Water slowly breaks down the lowest layers of reed, so islanders keep adding fresh reeds on top. On the busier islands, that means a new layer about every three months, and more often in the rainy season.
claims.statement: The bottom reeds of the Uros islands rot, so fresh reeds are added on top; on busier islands roughly every three months, and more often in the rainy season.

claims.quote: Even with all that care, an island lasts around thirty years before people have to build a new one from scratch.
claims.statement: A well-maintained Uros floating island lasts about 30 years before a new one must be built from scratch.

claims.quote: According to a Stanford researcher quoted by Smithsonian, rotting reeds produce gases, including carbon dioxide and methane, and those gases may help keep the islands floating.
claims.statement: Stanford professor Robert Dunbar told Smithsonian that decaying totora reeds produce gases such as CO2 and methane, and Smithsonian notes such gases may help keep the islands buoyant.

claims.quote: The Uros have lived on this lake for hundreds of years. According to the most common account, they moved out onto floating islands when the Inca Empire expanded onto their land.
claims.statement: The Uros have lived on Lake Titicaca for hundreds of years; according to the common account, they took up residence on floating islands when the Incas expanded onto their land.

claims.quote: Smithsonian puts it simply: they made islands they could move if things got tense.
claims.statement: Smithsonian describes the Uros as building reed islands that could be moved if tensions arose.

claims.quote: sometimes with a carved animal head at the front
claims.statement: Some Uros reed boats feature carved animal or dragon heads at the front.

claims.quote: Under it all, the island itself sits on big floating blocks of totora roots. They are tied together with rope and anchored, so the island does not drift off in the night.
claims.statement: The base of each Uros island is made of floating blocks of totora roots tied together with rope and anchored, then covered with layers of cut reeds.

claims.quote: Lake Titicaca sits at about three thousand eight hundred and ten metres. That's around twelve thousand five hundred feet. Britannica calls it the world's highest lake navigable by large vessels.
claims.statement: Lake Titicaca lies at about 3,810 m (12,500 ft) and is described by Britannica as the world's highest lake navigable to large vessels.

claims.quote: The reed beds around these islands are part of the Titicaca National Reserve. It protects about thirty-seven thousand hectares of reeds, with around sixty kinds of birds and fourteen kinds of fish. The Uros have long used many of them for meat and eggs.
claims.statement: The Uros islands lie within the Titicaca National Reserve, which protects about 37,000 hectares of reed beds with some 60 bird species and 14 fish species, many used by the Uros for meat and eggs.

claims.quote: Islanders barter with merchants from Puno for meat and vegetables.
claims.statement: Uros islanders barter for meat and vegetables with merchants from Puno.

claims.quote: Discover magazine notes that clean water is limited on the islands.
claims.statement: Discover Magazine notes that life on the Uros islands includes limited access to clean water.

claims.quote: Then, after a devastating storm in nineteen eighty-six, Smithsonian reports, many Uros rebuilt their islands near Puno.
claims.statement: After a devastating storm in 1986, many Uros rebuilt their islands near Puno, according to Smithsonian.

claims.quote: Visitors now come by the hundreds of thousands. Families take turns opening their homes to show how reed life works, and around eighty percent of the local population works in tourism.
claims.statement: Hundreds of thousands of tourists visit the Uros islands; families take turns showing visitors their homes, and about 80 percent of the local population works in tourism.

claims.quote: At the twenty eleven census, according to Culture Trip, about twelve hundred Uros were living on sixty-two islands near Puno.
claims.statement: According to Culture Trip, a 2011 census counted about 1,200 Uros living on 62 artificial islands near Puno.

claims.quote: Many Uros also live in the city itself
claims.statement: Many Uros live in Puno, the largest Peruvian city on Lake Titicaca.

claims.quote: When tourism stopped during the pandemic, Discover magazine reported, the islands felt it hard.
claims.statement: Discover Magazine reported that the tourism-reliant Uros suffered from pandemic travel restrictions.

claims.quote: Most Uros today speak Aymara and Spanish, and their old Uru language has almost disappeared
claims.statement: Most Uros today speak Aymara and Spanish; the Uru language is nearly extinct.
